title: Why don’t you see the world blur when your eyes jump?
hook: Try watching your own eyes move in a mirror. You can’t.
summary: With each quick jump of the eyes, the brain briefly blocks visual processing, so the blur never reaches awareness.

cardBlocks.text: Look in a mirror and shift your gaze from one eye to the other: you will never see your eyes move, even though someone else can. These quick jumps of the eyes are called saccades. Because they are so fast, the image on the retina inevitably blurs during the movement.

Blurred images aren’t much use, and the brain selectively blocks visual processing during these jumps. This is saccadic suppression, first described in 1898. It starts even before the eye moves, so it can’t be triggered by the moving image: the brain itself switches it on.
With each jump of your gaze, the brain briefly turns vision off, which is why you never see the world blur.

deepDiveBlocks.text: In 2021, researchers at the University of Rochester showed that it also happens during microsaccades, tiny jumps of the gaze. Just before and just after the movement, participants couldn’t see targets even when looking straight at them. Vision at the centre of gaze, though, recovered quickly.

The details are still argued over. Two kinds of suppression were long described, but later tests suggest those explanations may not be right, and one study showed that motion can be detected during a saccade.

claims.text: Saccades are fast eye movements, and during them the image on the retina inevitably blurs.

claims.text: The brain selectively blocks visual processing during saccades: this is saccadic suppression.

support.excerpt: Saccadic masking, also known as (visual) saccadic suppression, is the phenomenon in visual perception where the brain selectively blocks visual processing during eye movements
